interview_metadata.name: Miranda Johnson
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Cleveland, Ohio, mostly on the west side before my family settled around Parma and then I eventually moved to Strongsville as an adult. My family is African-American, with roots in Alabama and Mississippi through my grandparents, who came north during the Great Migration for factory work and steadier schools. I grew up in a household where church, grades, and keeping your word mattered. My mother worked in medical billing at a hospital system, and my father worked maintenance for a manufacturing plant, so I saw both office discipline and hands-on problem solving. I was the kind of girl who liked math, color-coded notebooks, and pickup basketball with cousins after Sunday dinner. I went to public schools, was in choir, played some basketball, and learned early that being prepared made people take me seriously. I earned a bachelor's degree with a STEM focus, leaning into data analysis and systems thinking. After college I started in administrative support, then moved into operations because I liked fixing messy processes. Over time I became a first-line supervisor of office and administrative support workers, and I now lead a team, track productivity metrics, redesign workflows, train staff, and push digital tools that make work less chaotic. I have never been married and I do not have children, though I am close to my nieces, nephews, church family, and the girls and boys I coach through Cuyahoga Hoops. A major life event for me was learning how to stand up for myself in corporate spaces as a Black woman without shrinking my personality. Another was buying my townhouse in Strongsville, because it felt like I had built something stable on my own. These days my life is work, church choir, Zumba, youth basketball, hiking, reading mysteries, cooking healthier soul food, and trying to grow into an operations manager or director role.

follow_ups.question: When you think back to childhood, what did a normal week look like in your family?
follow_ups.response: School during the week, church choir rehearsal or Bible study, homework at the kitchen table, and family meals on Sundays. My parents were strict but loving, and there was always an auntie or cousin stopping by.

follow_ups.question: Who helped shape your sense that education and preparation mattered?
follow_ups.response: My mother most of all. She would say, 'Nobody can argue with the numbers if you know your numbers,' and that stuck with me in school and at work.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was about eight or nine years ago when I was working as a senior administrative coordinator. I was good at the job, but I kept seeing the same workflow problems repeat: duplicate forms, late reports, people manually entering data that could have been automated. A manager suggested I apply for a supervisory opening, but I was hesitant because I knew supervising meant conflict, visibility, and being judged differently. Around that same time I took a Lean Six Sigma course through work, and it clicked for me that my frustration could be turned into a skill set. I applied, interviewed with a binder full of process maps, and got the promotion. That decision changed my confidence. I stopped thinking of myself as just the person who kept things organized and started seeing myself as someone who could lead change.

follow_ups.question: What was the first change you made after becoming a supervisor?
follow_ups.response: I standardized our intake tracker and built a dashboard so people could see pending requests by age and priority. It cut down on finger-pointing because the work was visible.

follow_ups.question: Was anyone skeptical of you stepping into that role?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a couple of older coworkers were. I had to prove I was not just coming in with spreadsheets but that I understood their workload and would listen.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I remember sitting in my car after work, looking at the job posting on my phone, and deciding that fear was not a good enough reason to stay put.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk it through with anyone?
follow_ups.response: I talked to my mother and to a mentor from a Black professional networking group. Both told me I was already doing parts of the job unofficially.

follow_ups.question: What made the decision feel risky?
follow_ups.response: Being responsible for people, not just tasks. I knew if the team struggled, that would land on me.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. Formal leadership coaching would have helped. My employer eventually offered training, but in the beginning I had to learn a lot by trial and error.

follow_ups.question: What kind of support would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A structured mentor, especially another Black woman in operations leadership, would have helped me navigate office politics.

follow_ups.question: Do you try to provide that now?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. I mentor younger staff and tell them the unwritten rules instead of making them guess.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I have never been married, I am not living with a partner, and I do not have children. My family is still very important, though. My mother, Denise, lives in the Cleveland area, and we talk almost every day, usually after work while I am making dinner. My father, Robert, is retired and still acts like he can fix anything with one toolbox and a cup of coffee. I have an older brother, Marcus, who has two kids, and I am very involved as Auntie Miranda. I go to their games, help with school projects when I can, and I am the person who buys practical birthday gifts with one fun thing tucked in. My extended family is close too, especially around holidays, church events, and Juneteenth. Being single at 40 sometimes brings comments from relatives, but I have built a full life. I date occasionally, but I am not trying to force a relationship just to satisfy other people's timeline.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents and brother?
follow_ups.response: My parents about once a week, usually Sunday dinner or after church. My brother's family maybe two or three times a month, more during basketball season.

follow_ups.question: What role do you play in family gatherings?
follow_ups.response: I am the planner. I make the signup list, coordinate dishes, and somehow still end up baking sweet-potato pie.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate family is my parents and my brother. I am also close to my sister-in-law, Tasha, and my niece and nephew.

follow_ups.question: What are your niece and nephew like?
follow_ups.response: My niece is artsy and dramatic in a good way, and my nephew is sports all day. They keep me laughing.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with them regularly?
follow_ups.response: Not daily, but I help with rides, games, and school projects when my brother and Tasha need backup.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes, I have a solid circle. My closest friends are Keisha, who I met in college, and Lauren, who is in my book club. I also have church friends from choir, women I see at Zumba twice a week, and a running club group that meets early on Saturdays. I am not in a serious romantic relationship right now, though I have gone on a few dates through friends and apps. My social life is active but scheduled. If it is not on my calendar, it probably will not happen.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your friends usually do together?
follow_ups.response: Book club, brunch after church, Cavs watch parties, art festivals, and sometimes just cooking at someone's house.

follow_ups.question: Who do you call when something is really bothering you?
follow_ups.response: Keisha first, then my mom. Keisha lets me vent, and my mom moves straight to solutions.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Strongsville, Ohio, zip code 44136, in a townhouse community that is quiet and pretty convenient. It is suburban, with shopping centers, grocery stores, gyms, and restaurants within a short drive. I like that I can get to work, church, and my parents without too much trouble, and Cuyahoga Valley National Park is close enough for weekend hikes. My immediate neighbors are a mix of young professionals, retirees, and families. People wave, shovel sidewalks, and mostly mind their business. It is not as culturally rich as some parts of Cleveland, but it is stable and practical.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually shop nearby?
follow_ups.response: Giant Eagle, Heinen's when I want better produce, Target for basics, and sometimes local farm stands in season.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few. I know the retired couple next door and a single mom across the way, but I would not say it is a block-party-every-week place.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. I will take walks in the evening, though I still stay aware, keep my porch light on, and do not act careless just because it is suburban.

follow_ups.question: Have you had any safety issues there?
follow_ups.response: Nothing major, just a few car break-ins in nearby lots that made everyone more careful.

follow_ups.question: Does being a Black woman affect how safe you feel there?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. I feel physically safe, but I am aware of when I stand out in certain spaces.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience, quiet, and a good base for my routines. The downside is that I sometimes have to drive back toward Cleveland for the church, cultural events, restaurants, and community spaces that feel more like home.

follow_ups.question: What would you change if you could?
follow_ups.response: More walkable restaurants and more Black-owned businesses nearby.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Stability, manageable costs, and being close enough to family without being in everybody's business.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live by myself in my townhouse. No partner, no children, no roommate. I like having my own space because my workday is people-heavy, so when I come home I need quiet. My place has a small backyard garden, a kitchen I actually use, and a spare room that is half home office and half storage for coaching supplies and choir music.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone stay over regularly?
follow_ups.response: My niece might stay one night during school breaks, but that is occasional, not regular.

follow_ups.question: How do you use your home during the week?
follow_ups.response: Meal prep on Sundays, remote admin work sometimes, reading at night, and a lot of laundry after workouts.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me permanently.

follow_ups.question: Any planned changes to that?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Would you consider a roommate?
follow_ups.response: Only in a serious emergency. I like my space.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my niece stays overnight, or a friend might stay after a late event, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: How often would you say that happens?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep a guest space ready?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I keep the spare room usable even though it collects paperwork.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is one?
follow_ups.response: Yes, just one.

follow_ups.question: Any pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets right now.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am usually up around 5:45. Two mornings a week I run with a local group before work, and other days I stretch, make coffee, and check my calendar. I work roughly 8:00 to 5:00, with some variation depending on meetings or deadlines. Monday is planning and staff assignments, Tuesday and Thursday often have workflow reviews, and Friday I try to close out reports. After work I may go to Zumba, choir rehearsal, youth basketball practice, or book club depending on the day. Saturdays are for running, errands, coaching games, or hiking. Sundays are church, family dinner, meal prep, and getting my clothes and lunches lined up for the week.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:30, though if I get into a mystery novel it can become midnight.

follow_ups.question: What is the most packed day?
follow_ups.response: Thursday, because work meetings, Zumba, and sometimes choir all stack up.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work full time as an operations supervisor for an office administrative team. My job is basically making sure requests, documents, schedules, and support functions move through the system accurately and on time. I supervise staff, build reports, handle escalations, review performance metrics, train people on software, and work with managers on process improvements. My normal schedule is weekdays, about 8 to 5, but I can shift earlier or later if there is a project rollout or staff coverage issue. I do not have a second paid job. Coaching youth basketball is volunteer work.

follow_ups.question: Do you work from home at all?
follow_ups.response: Usually one day a week if coverage allows, mostly for reporting, documentation, and project work.

follow_ups.question: What tools do you use most?
follow_ups.response: Excel, Power BI, shared workflow systems, Teams, Outlook, and sometimes basic SQL queries when I need to pull data.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my parents with technology and appointments when needed, especially online portals and insurance paperwork. I volunteer at the community center through basketball and occasional career workshops. I keep a garden in the warm months with herbs, tomatoes, peppers, and greens. I also do a lot of meal prep because if I do not plan, I end up eating crackers and leftovers at odd hours.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually meal prep?
follow_ups.response: Turkey collard greens, quinoa gumbo, roasted vegetables, grilled chicken, and breakfast egg cups.

follow_ups.question: How often do you volunteer outside coaching?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month, more around Juneteenth or school events.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I added more structured studying for PMP certification, usually two evenings a week for an hour. Work has also been more intense because we are moving more processes into digital forms and dashboards. I used to do Zumba three times a week, but now it is usually twice so I can fit studying and coaching. I have also been trying to protect one quiet evening at home because I realized every night was becoming an obligation.

follow_ups.question: Which evening do you try to protect?
follow_ups.response: Wednesday, if I can. I cook, water plants, and read.

follow_ups.question: Has the new study routine been hard to keep?
follow_ups.response: Some weeks yes. I have to treat it like a meeting or it disappears.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children. For my niece and nephew, I help occasionally, but I am not part of their daily school routine. They have school, homework, and sports or arts depending on the season. My nephew plays basketball, and my niece has art club and choir. I show up when I can, especially for games and performances.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever handle school pickup?
follow_ups.response: Only as backup if my brother and sister-in-law are stuck.

follow_ups.question: Does coaching overlap with family time?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, because my nephew has come to clinics, but I try not to make him feel like I am his coach all the time.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have mostly been traffic stops, but they stay with you. I have been pulled over twice, once for a taillight and once for speeding, and both times I was very deliberate with my hands and words. Nothing violent happened, but I felt that tightness in my chest because you never know how quickly a normal stop can turn. I also have cousins and male friends who have had more tense experiences.

follow_ups.question: What do you do during a traffic stop?
follow_ups.response: Window down, hands visible, license ready only when asked, and I narrate what I am doing.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone teach you that?
follow_ups.response: My parents did, especially my dad. It was part of growing up Black in America.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: At community events, I have seen both sides. Some officers are helpful with traffic and youth programs, but there is also a feeling that certain groups get watched more closely.

follow_ups.question: Have you interacted with police through coaching?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly at community center events. I appreciate officers who build relationships before there is a problem.

follow_ups.question: What makes an interaction feel respectful?
follow_ups.response: Tone, explaining what is happening, and not treating people like suspects by default.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have a cousin who was arrested years ago for a nonviolent drug-related issue, and the court process was hard on the family financially and emotionally.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how you see the justice system?
follow_ups.response: Yes. It showed me how one mistake can follow someone for years, especially when they do not have money for good legal help.

follow_ups.question: Is he doing better now?
follow_ups.response: Yes, he works steadily now, but rebuilding took time.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections, midterms, and most local elections. I will not pretend I know every judicial race perfectly, but I do research before I vote. My parents treated voting like a responsibility, and church also reinforced that. I have voted early when work was busy, and I remind friends about registration deadlines.

follow_ups.question: How do you research candidates?
follow_ups.response: League of Women Voters guides, local news, candidate websites, and conversations with people I trust.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever volunteer politically?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally I have done voter registration tables, but I am not a campaign regular.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as a practical Democrat, maybe center-left but very strong on civil rights, voting rights, health care access, public education, and workplace equity. I believe government has a role in making sure people have a fair chance, but I also care about whether programs are actually managed well. My operations brain shows up in politics; I want good intentions and good execution. I support police accountability, reproductive rights, and investment in communities that have been overlooked. I am not anti-business, but I do think companies should pay people fairly and create real pathways for advancement, especially for women and people of color. I also care about small things that affect daily life, like roads, schools, libraries, parks, and whether city services actually answer the phone.

follow_ups.question: What local issues matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Schools, public safety with accountability, small business support, and maintaining parks and community centers.

follow_ups.question: Do your coworkers share your politics?
follow_ups.response: It is mixed. I am careful at work, but people know where I stand on inclusion and fair treatment.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on local government and implementation. When I was younger, I mostly followed national races. Now I pay more attention to school boards, city councils, judges, and county decisions because those affect everyday life quickly. I have also become less patient with symbolic diversity statements that do not include budgets, metrics, and accountability. If an organization says equity matters, I want to see who gets promoted, who gets contracts, and who is in the room when decisions are made.

follow_ups.question: What caused that shift toward local politics?
follow_ups.response: Seeing how much local decisions affected pandemic response, schools, policing, and community programs.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with my parents and brother, though we try not to let it take over Sunday dinner.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me a lot. Not because the issues were new to me, but because the wider public attention made conversations unavoidable. Seeing names and videos over and over was painful, and it made me think about my father, brother, nephew, and the young people I coach. It also pushed me to be more vocal at work about equity, not just in big statements but in hiring panels, promotion pathways, and how we handle complaints.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your emotional state?
follow_ups.response: Yes, there were weeks when I felt angry and exhausted, especially after watching the same arguments repeat online.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your work conversations?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I helped organize a listening session and pushed for action items instead of just a statement.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as bigger than policing alone. Policing is one part, but there is also housing, schools, health care, hiring, and whose pain gets believed. I support accountability and training, but I also believe communities need resources before crisis points. With kids I coach, I think about confidence and safety together. I want them to feel powerful on the court and careful in the world, which is a heavy message to carry.

follow_ups.question: How do you discuss these issues with young people?
follow_ups.response: Age-appropriately. I talk about respect, knowing your rights, staying calm, and also not accepting unfair treatment as normal.

follow_ups.question: What solutions feel most important?
follow_ups.response: Accountability, community investment, mental health response teams, and transparency in stops and discipline.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country wants progress without discomfort, and that is not realistic. At work, in neighborhoods, and in schools, race shows up in who is trusted, who gets second chances, and whose leadership style is labeled aggressive versus confident. I also see beautiful things: Black professionals mentoring each other, young people speaking clearly, Juneteenth events growing, and more people learning history. But backlash is real too. I try to stay grounded and not let every headline steal my peace.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel race most in your own life?
follow_ups.response: Professional settings. I pay attention to tone, appearance, and preparation because I know mistakes may be judged harder.

follow_ups.question: What gives you hope?
follow_ups.response: Young people and community networks. They are direct, creative, and less willing to accept old excuses.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and friends, attended a local peaceful march, donated to community bail and youth organizations, and pushed workplace conversations. I am not at every protest, but I am not silent either.

follow_ups.question: What was the march like?
follow_ups.response: It was emotional but organized, with families, clergy, students, and people holding signs downtown.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I try to share resources more than argue in comment sections.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My family talks about it openly. My parents connect it to what they and my grandparents experienced, and my brother thinks about his son. My friends are mostly engaged, though people respond differently. Some go to protests, some donate, some focus on school board meetings or workplace advocacy. In my church, there has been prayer, discussion, and voter registration work tied to justice issues.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone close to you disagreed strongly?
follow_ups.response: A few coworkers see it differently, but in my close circle most people agree on the basics of accountability.

follow_ups.question: Do these conversations drain you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, yes. I have learned to step back when I am repeating myself to someone not listening.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is good. I am active with Zumba, running, hiking, and coaching, and I try to cook in a way that respects soul food flavors without making every meal heavy. I watch my blood pressure because it runs in my family, but I have not been diagnosed with hypertension. I carry stress in my shoulders and sometimes get tension headaches. My annual checkups have been normal, and I try to stay ahead of things.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually four or five days a week between running, Zumba, and hiking or coaching.

follow_ups.question: What health goal are you working on?
follow_ups.response: Better sleep and stretching more consistently.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I genuinely like group fitness and cooking. Zumba feels social, not like punishment, and running club keeps me accountable. It is harder when work gets intense and I eat late or skip stretching. Also, I love biscuits and sweet potato pie, so moderation is a real discipline.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit sticks best?
follow_ups.response: Sunday meal prep. If containers are ready, I make better choices.

follow_ups.question: What habit slips first?
follow_ups.response: Sleep. I stay up reading or finishing one more work task.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing major like a diagnosis or broken bone. I had a knee strain from running last year, probably from adding mileage too quickly, and I had to back off for a few weeks. I did physical therapy exercises at home, got better shoes, and became more careful about warmups. I also had a stressful period where headaches were more frequent, and my doctor basically told me my body was asking for rest.

follow_ups.question: Did the knee strain affect coaching?
follow_ups.response: A little. I demonstrated less and had assistant coaches help with drills.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor for the headaches?
follow_ups.response: Yes, at a routine appointment. No serious issue, just stress, screen time, and tight muscles.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously interfered with work. Stress can make me less patient if I do not manage it, but I have sick time and enough flexibility to handle appointments.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work because of health?
follow_ups.response: Only normal sick days or appointments, nothing extended.

follow_ups.question: What helps you keep functioning during stressful weeks?
follow_ups.response: Lists, early bedtime when I can, and moving my body even briefly.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, mainly with my parents getting older. My mom manages Type 2 diabetes, and my dad has high blood pressure and some knee arthritis. They are independent, but I help with appointments, portal messages, medication questions, and making sure they understand insurance letters. It is not full-time caregiving, but it is in the background. I also think about how quickly that could change.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help with medical tasks?
follow_ups.response: A few times a month, more if there is a new bill or appointment.

follow_ups.question: Does your brother help too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with physical tasks and rides. I handle more paperwork.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have employer health insurance, so I am fortunate compared with many people, but it is still frustrating. Finding specialists, understanding bills, and waiting for appointments can be a lot. I have delayed dental work before because the out-of-pocket cost was high, but I have not gone without major medical care. For my parents, the hardest part is coordinating information between doctors and making sure prescriptions are covered.

follow_ups.question: What care did you delay?
follow_ups.response: A dental crown. I waited a few months so I could use FSA money.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust your doctors?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, but I ask questions and bring notes because rushed visits miss things.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing extreme, but we use home remedies alongside regular care. Ginger tea, honey, steam, Epsom salt baths, heating pads, and herbal teas are common in my family. My grandmother believed in a lot of kitchen medicine. I still go to doctors, but I do believe comfort care and food traditions matter too.

follow_ups.question: What do you use ginger for?
follow_ups.response: Stomach upset, colds, and just because I like the warmth of it.

follow_ups.question: Do you tell doctors about supplements or remedies?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially if it is anything beyond tea or food.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, maybe wine at book club or a cocktail at dinner, but not as my main coping strategy. When I am stressed I am more likely to over-schedule myself, snack late at night, or clean the kitchen at 11 p.m. I have learned that exercise, prayer, and talking to a friend work better.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three drinks in a typical month, sometimes more around holidays.

follow_ups.question: What is your stress snack?
follow_ups.response: Leftover biscuits. I wish that were not so true, but it is.

follow_ups.question: Were they married then?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was the household stable?
follow_ups.response: Yes, structured and stable.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My older brother, Marcus. No one else lived with us full time.

follow_ups.question: Did extended family stay often?
follow_ups.response: Cousins visited a lot, but they did not live with us.

follow_ups.question: Were you close with your brother then?
follow_ups.response: We argued like siblings, but yes, we were close.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: My dad completed high school and some vocational training.

follow_ups.question: What kind of training?
follow_ups.response: Maintenance and mechanical skills through work programs.

follow_ups.question: Did he value college for you?
follow_ups.response: Very much.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: My mom completed some college and a medical billing/coding certificate.

follow_ups.question: Did she continue training while working?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she took certificate courses.

follow_ups.question: Did she encourage your education?
follow_ups.response: Constantly.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was she full time?
follow_ups.response: Most of the time, yes.

follow_ups.question: Did her work affect household routines?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we had organized mornings and planned meals because everyone was busy.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She worked in medical billing and coding. She processed insurance claims, checked patient account information, corrected coding issues, and followed up on payments. Her work required accuracy and patience, and I think that influenced my own detail-oriented style.

follow_ups.question: Did she talk about work at home?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially about paperwork and how one wrong code could delay everything.

follow_ups.question: Did you learn office skills from her?
follow_ups.response: Yes, organization, documentation, and double-checking.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a hospital system and later a medical office billing department. They provided health care, and her part was making sure services were coded, billed, and paid correctly.

follow_ups.question: Was it a large employer?
follow_ups.response: Yes, part of a larger health system.

follow_ups.question: Did that shape your interest in health care operations?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. It made me appreciate how much administration affects patient experience.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Was he steady in that work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very steady.

follow_ups.question: Did he work shifts?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes early shifts and occasional overtime.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad worked in maintenance for a manufacturing plant. He repaired equipment, handled building maintenance, checked systems, responded to breakdowns, and made sure operations could keep running. He was practical and calm under pressure.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you hands-on skills?
follow_ups.response: Yes, basic tools, troubleshooting, and not panicking when something breaks.

follow_ups.question: Did he like the work?
follow_ups.response: He took pride in being reliable, even when the work was hard.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: It was a manufacturing plant in the Cleveland area that made industrial components. I do not remember every product detail, but it was the kind of place where machines, schedules, and safety mattered every day.

follow_ups.question: Did the plant feel connected to Cleveland history?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very much. Manufacturing work was part of my family's path into the middle class.

follow_ups.question: Did layoffs affect your family?
follow_ups.response: Not directly in a major way, but there was always awareness that plants could change quickly.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now I hope I am in an operations manager or director of administration role, preferably in a midsize company or health care organization where the work has real purpose. I want my PMP and Six Sigma Green Belt finished, and I want to lead cross-functional projects instead of only managing one team. I also hope to be mentoring Black women more formally, not just giving advice in hallway conversations. Personally, I want to stay close to family, keep my health strong, travel more, and maybe be in a committed relationship if it is the right person. I would like to visit Savannah in spring, keep singing, keep coaching, and have a home that feels peaceful. I want growth, but I do not want success to cost me my joy.

follow_ups.question: What would tell you that you had made it professionally?
follow_ups.response: Having authority to shape systems, develop people, and make inclusive leadership normal instead of decorative.

follow_ups.question: What do you want to remain the same?
follow_ups.response: My connection to family, church, community, and the parts of me that laugh loudly and show up for people.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value faith, family, integrity, community, and growth. I value being dependable, but I am learning that being dependable does not mean being available for everything. I care about excellence because my parents and grandparents worked too hard for me to coast. I also value joy: music, good food, movement, books, laughter, and those moments when people feel seen because you made room for them.

follow_ups.question: What value guides your decisions most often?
follow_ups.response: Integrity. I need to respect how I handled something, even if the outcome is imperfect.

follow_ups.question: What do you hope people feel around you?
follow_ups.response: That I am honest, prepared, warm, and in their corner.

summaries.demographer: Miranda Johnson is a 40-year-old Black/African-American woman living alone in an owned townhouse in Strongsville, Ohio, with no spouse, cohabiting partner, or children (Q05, Q11, Q84, Q89). She was born in Cleveland and raised in the Cleveland area by both parents with one older brother in a stable, education-oriented household (Q87-Q99). She has a bachelor's degree and works full time as an operations supervisor, placing her in a stable single-income professional household with employer benefits and moderate assets such as homeownership and retirement savings (Q65, Q72, Q76, Q83). Her life course is strongly shaped by family, church, Great Migration heritage, and upward mobility through education and administrative leadership (Q01, Q47, Q108).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Miranda shows high planning orientation, future focus, and risk management through spreadsheet budgeting, automatic savings, certification study, and emergency funds (Q57, Q61, Q62, Q82). She responds to uncertainty by creating routines, lists, sinking funds, and documented workflows, both at home and work (Q15, Q50, Q65). Her choices are identity-linked: she invests time in church, mentoring, Black professional advancement, and youth coaching because these reinforce community obligations and self-concept (Q04, Q17, Q29, Q108). She is cautious but not deprived; she spends on fitness, food, family, and travel while cutting discretionary purchases when expenses rise (Q56-Q60).
summaries.political_scientist: Miranda is a fairly strong Democrat with center-left, pragmatic views focused on civil rights, voting access, public education, health care, workplace equity, and competent implementation (Q23-Q25, Q95-Q96). She votes regularly, researches candidates, and pays increasing attention to local institutions such as school boards, judges, and city government (Q23, Q25). Her politics are rooted in racial identity, church community, family history, and direct workplace experience with representation and accountability (Q26-Q30). She has participated in peaceful protest, donated to community causes, supported voter registration, and organized workplace equity conversations, indicating high civic engagement but not full-time campaign activism (Q23, Q29, Q47).
summaries.psychologist: Miranda presents as conscientious, socially vibrant, achievement-oriented, and emotionally self-aware, with a strong need for order, excellence, and meaningful contribution (Q01, Q02, Q65, Q109). She copes with stress through exercise, prayer, social support, scheduling, cooking, and occasional journaling, while recognizing tendencies toward over-responsibility and anxious rumination (Q43-Q45, Q50). Her self-concept combines warmth and discipline: she wants to be dependable, prepared, honest, and in people's corner, but she is learning boundaries (Q43, Q50, Q109). Family, faith, Black womanhood, and professional competence are central to her identity and motivation (Q01, Q28, Q47, Q108).
